title: Sanquhar chequerboard mitts
subtitle: Full mittens in the Sanquhar chequerboard tradition, using a two-colour chequered stitch.
excerpt: Full mittens in the Sanquhar knitting tradition, worked in a two-colour alternating chequerboard pattern throughout. DK weight, worked in the round, afterthought thumb. Sized for hand circumferences of 18, 20, and 22 cm.
sourceNotes: The Sanquhar chequerboard is a traditional two-colour knitting pattern from Sanquhar, Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland. The chequerboard pattern (alternating 1-stitch squares of two colours) is documented in Michael Pearson's Traditional Knitting (1984) and in the Sanquhar Glove pattern archive at Dumfries Museum, all out of copyright.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts x 28 rounds = 10 x 10 cm in stranded colourwork on 3.75 mm needles.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Hand circumference 18 (20, 22) cm with 1 to 2 cm negative ease.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Scottish tradition of two-colour knitting from the town of Sanquhar in Dumfriesshire. Patterns are based on geometric repeats, most commonly a chequerboard and a duke pattern. The work uses alternating dark and light wool, typically black and white.

A thumb opening made by working the thumb stitches in waste yarn during the hand, then returning after the hand is complete. The waste yarn is removed to reveal live stitches which are picked up and worked as the thumb.
A method for knitting small circumferences in the round on one long circular needle. The cable is pulled into a loop at the midpoint so each half of the stitches sits on its own needle tip.

content.text: Full mittens in the
Sanquhar knitting
tradition, worked in a two-colour chequerboard pattern throughout, with an
afterthought thumb
. Sized for hand circumferences of 18, 20, and 22 cm.

The chequerboard alternates one MC stitch and one CC stitch, then swaps on the next round so the colours form squares. Both yarns are carried throughout and the floats are very short (always 1 stitch) so there is no snagging risk. The construction uses
magic loop
on a long circular. Budget about 70 g (155 m / 170 yards) of each colour, both DK. Traditional Sanquhar uses black and white; any high-contrast pair works.
What you need

items.name: MC (main colour, dark)
items.qty: 70 g (about 155 m / 170 yards) of DK-weight wool

items.name: CC (contrast colour, light)
items.qty: 70 g (about 155 m / 170 yards) of the same yarn

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 3.75 mm (UK 9 / US 5) circular needle, at least 80 cm cable, for magic loop

items.name: Stitch markers
items.qty: 3: 1 for beginning of round, 1 for thumb, 1 for top shaping midpoint

items.name: Waste yarn
items.qty: About 30 cm of smooth contrasting yarn for the thumb

content.text: Gauge
22 stitches and 28 rounds to 10 cm in stranded colourwork on 3.75 mm needles. The short floats in chequerboard keep the gauge close to that of stranded colourwork generally.
Chequerboard pattern

items.name: Round 1
items.qty: *k1 MC, k1 CC*; repeat to end.

items.name: Round 2
items.qty: *k1 CC, k1 MC*; repeat to end.

content.text: The colour sequence simply swaps on every round. Both yarns must be carried across the back at all times; hold MC in the left hand and CC in the right (or use your preferred two-handed method).
Pattern
Before you cast on, circle your size. Every stitch count reads S (M, L) for hand circumferences 18 (20, 22) cm.
Cast on and cuff

Using both MC and CC held together, cast on 40 (44, 48) stitches using the long-tail cast-on with one colour as the thumb strand and one as the finger strand. This produces a two-colour cast-on edge. Join to work in the round. Work 6 rounds of 1x1 rib alternating MC and CC (k1 MC, p1 CC). Begin the chequerboard pattern.
Hand body

Continue in chequerboard for 12 (14, 14) rounds. Place the afterthought thumb: work the first 10 (11, 12) stitches with waste yarn (in chequerboard pattern), slip back, and work in chequerboard to end. Continue chequerboard for 24 (26, 28) more rounds.
Top shaping

Place a marker at the midpoint. Continue the chequerboard on the plain stitches and work decreases in MC only. Decrease round: k1 MC, ssk MC, continue chequerboard to 3 before midpoint, k2tog MC, k1 MC, SM, k1 MC, ssk MC, continue to last 3, k2tog MC, k1 MC. Plain chequerboard round. Repeat until 8 stitches remain. Draw MC through and close.
Thumb
Remove waste yarn. Pick up 10 (11, 12) stitches above and 10 (11, 12) below. Continue chequerboard for 14 (16, 16) rounds. Work 4 rounds of 1x1 MC rib. Bind off in rib.
Common faults

Chequerboard misaligns: the round 2 colour sequence matches round 1 instead of swapping. On round 2, the first stitch must be CC where it was MC on round 1. Mark the first stitch of each round to track the swap.
Tension uneven between the two yarns: one hand is pulling harder than the other. Practice carrying both yarns at the same tension using a yarn guide or adjusting your finger positions.
Finishing
Weave each colour tail in the matching colour on the wrong side. Block by soaking and pinning flat to square up the chequerboard.
Care
Hand wash in cool water. Wash dark and light colours separately on the first wash if either colour is likely to bleed. Lay flat to dry.
What to try next

The traditional Sanquhar glove adds individual finger tubes, which require the same chequerboard technique. The Fair Isle fingerless mitts pattern uses a related two-colour structure at the same gauge.
